canonical_topic: Crude oil as a global market vs. refined products as regional markets
definition: Crude oil trades as a roughly uniform global commodity that can be redirected between regions in response to price differences, while refined products like gasoline trade in fragmented regional markets with limited cross-border substitutability.
core_idea: Because tanker shipments of crude can be redirected wherever prices are highest and different refineries can generally process crude meant for other regions, crude oil prices tend to converge globally; refined products lack this flexibility because international transport infrastructure for finished products is limited and local environmental regulations force region-specific formulations, so their prices and specifications vary substantially by location.
key_points: Crude oil is approximately the same product at approximately the same price everywhere it trades, because tankers can be redirected to wherever the price is higher.
Refineries in different regions (e.g. northeastern U.S. and northern Europe) can generally each process crude oil originally intended for the other.

Refined products are historically refined close to their final consumption point rather than shipped internationally in bulk, partly because locating refineries outside industrialized countries was considered risky.
There is limited international infrastructure for transporting finished petroleum products in bulk, so cross-border trade volumes are much lower than for crude.

Local environmental regulations fragment refined product markets further — e.g. North American gasoline formulation differs from European, and formulations can even differ within a country (California vs. New York).
relationships: Regional formulation regulation drives regional price divergence in refined products
Global crude arbitrage keeps crude prices converged across regions
trading_implications: Crude oil price differentials across regions should compress quickly via tanker redirection; persistent regional refined-product price gaps are more structural and regulation-driven, not arbitraged away as easily.
caveats: Assuming refined product markets behave like crude oil's global market; the author stresses they are fragmented regional markets instead.
